C0.quote: We interpret objective functions as rules that take an approval profile
C0.note: Borderline case. Axis rules aggregate voters' approval ballots into a collective output (an ordering, or axis). The paper analyses them with social choice methods, though the output is a summary axis rather than a winner.

C1.loc: Abstract, p. 2757; Sec. 5, p. 2760; Sec. 6, p. 2762
C1.quote: compare 5 different axis selection rules axiomatically
C1.note: AL: Theorem 1 (NP-completeness). SI: Sec. 6.1 synthetic data. EM: Sec. 6.2-6.3, French election surveys and US Supreme Court data.

C2.1.quote: An approval profile P is a collection of n approval ballots

C2.2.quote: An approval ballot is a non-empty subset of candidates A ⊆ C.
C2.2.note: Ranking-based rules (VD-rank, FT-rank) appear only as comparison baselines in the experiments.

C2.3.quote: Each candidate and voter x ∈ C ∪ V is associated with a position
C2.3.note: The synthetic model gives voters positions and noisy estimates of candidate positions. Sec. 4 also discusses voters not approving candidates they do not know.

C2.4.quote: a voter i might not approve a candidate c because
C2.4.note: Positions p(v) and ballots have separate notation in the noise model, and the text allows ballots to deviate from what would be an 'error-free' approval.

C3.1.note: No strategic voting is considered anywhere in the paper.

C3.2.note: No statement that ballots equal held attitudes. The paper instead discusses errors and noise in ballots.

C4.1.note: No utility, welfare or satisfaction notions are used for voters. The 'cost' is the cost an axis incurs per ballot, not a voter's cost.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' appears only in a cited reference title.

C5.1.note: Rules are evaluated by axioms and by distance to ground-truth or reference axes, not by welfare or representation criteria.

VOT.quote_behav: Voters approve (resp. rank) candidates based on their estimations.
VOT.note: Ballots are exogenous in the axiomatic part and generated by a noise model in the simulations.

claims.quote: Our rules will find an axis in a principled way.
this will help with selecting a good objective function.
shows its normative appeal among the entire class of scoring rules

C9.1.note: Claims concern which axis rule should be used, including in practice by pollsters.

C9.2.quote: an ideological left-right axis such that each voter approves adjacent
C9.2.note: The claims rest on axioms defined over ballots. The needed interpretive assumption, that approvals of ideologically adjacent candidates form intervals, is stated.

C10.1.note: No explicit statement that the rule is studied only as a function of submitted inputs.
